title: Henna: Temporary Art on Skin
summary: How henna, a plant-based dye, is used to create temporary decorative patterns on hands and feet at celebrations across many cultures, and how the designs are applied and fade.
poll: Temporary body art like henna is a meaningful way to celebrate a special occasion.

versions.title: Henna Designs
versions.text:
Have you seen brown designs on a hand? That is henna. Henna comes from a plant.

People pick leaves off the plant. They dry the leaves. Then they grind them into a powder.

They mix the powder with water. This makes a paste. The paste is brown or green.

A person puts the paste on the skin. They make a design on the hand. It can take a long time.

The paste must stay on the skin. It needs time to dry. Then people wash it off.

The skin turns red-brown! It is not a real tattoo. It will not stay.

People use henna at happy times. They use it at weddings. They use it on Eid, too.

After some weeks, the design fades. Then skin looks plain again.

versions.title: The Art of Henna

Have you ever seen intricate red-brown patterns painted on a hand or foot? This kind of temporary body art is called henna, and it comes from a plant, Lawsonia inermis, that grows in warm places across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

To make henna dye, people harvest leaves off the henna plant and allow them to dry fully in the sun. Once dry, workers grind the leaves into a fine, green powder that holds a natural red-brown dye called lawsone, which gives henna its staining color.

That powder is then mixed with water, and often a little lemon juice or tea, in order to make a thick paste. The paste looks dark green or brown while wet, long before it dries completely on the skin's surface.

A skilled henna artist applies the paste onto the skin, piping it through a small cone or plastic bottle. She draws a detailed pattern on the hands and feet, and the work can take quite a long time when the design is complex.

The paste must stay on the skin long enough to dry and set, which usually takes several hours or sometimes even overnight. After that, the dry paste is brushed or washed away, showing the finished pattern that was hidden underneath.

The skin has turned a rich red-brown color! This temporary mark will not stay on the skin for good, unlike a real tattoo, since it only colors the outer layer of skin cells.

People love using henna during happy celebrations, such as weddings, and many families also apply henna at the feast of Eid, keeping a custom that goes back many years across numerous lands.

After roughly one to three weeks, the pattern slowly fades as old skin wears off and is replaced, and the skin eventually goes back to its normal color.

versions.title: Henna: An Enduring Art
versions.text:
Anyone who looks closely at the intricate red-brown patterns on a hand or foot can see why henna remains a lasting form of temporary body art. It comes from a plant, Lawsonia inermis, that grows in warm places across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

To produce the dye, growers harvest the leaves of the henna plant and allow them to dry completely under the sun. Once fully dry, the leaves are ground into a fine, green powder containing a natural reddish-brown pigment called lawsone, which is responsible for the distinctive staining color.

That pigment-rich powder is then combined with water, and often a little lemon juice or tea, to create a smooth, thick paste. This paste typically appears dark green or deep brown while still wet, long before it dries completely upon the skin's surface.

A skilled henna artisan applies the paste onto a person's skin, piping it through a small cone or plastic bottle to draw remarkably intricate, detailed patterns across the hands and feet. Producing these elaborate patterns can require a considerable amount of time.

The paste must remain on the skin long enough to dry completely and set, a process that usually takes several hours or sometimes an entire night. Afterward, the dry, crumbling paste is gently brushed or washed away, revealing the finished design that had been hidden beneath it.

The skin beneath has turned a rich reddish-brown color! This temporary stain will never remain on the skin indefinitely, since the pigment only colors the outermost layer of skin cells.

People especially cherish using henna during joyful celebrations, where the designs often carry symbolic meanings of happiness or blessing, and many families also apply henna during the holiday of Eid.

After roughly one to three weeks, the henna pattern gradually fades away as old skin cells naturally wear off and are steadily replaced, and the skin returns to its ordinary color.

versions.title: Henna: An Enduring Art
versions.text:
Anyone who looks closely at the intricate red-brown patterns on a hand or foot can readily appreciate why henna remains among the most enduring and widespread forms of temporary body art practiced throughout much of the world, a tradition originating from a flowering plant, Lawsonia inermis, that flourishes in warm climates across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

To produce the dye, growers carefully harvest the leaves of the henna plant and allow them to dry thoroughly and completely under the intense sun. Once fully dried, the leaves are ground into a fine, green powder containing a natural reddish-brown pigment called lawsone, which is responsible for the plant's distinctive staining properties and has been genuinely prized for many centuries.

That pigment-rich powder is subsequently combined with ordinary water, and frequently a small amount of lemon juice or tea, to produce a smooth, remarkably thick paste. This paste typically appears dark green or deep brown while still wet, long before it eventually dries completely upon the skin's surface.

A genuinely skilled henna artisan carefully applies the paste onto a person's skin, piping it through a small cone or plastic bottle to render remarkably intricate, highly detailed patterns across the hands, feet, and sometimes even the arms. Producing these elaborate patterns can require a truly considerable investment of time and patience.

The paste must remain on the skin long enough to dry completely and properly set, a process that usually requires several hours or, in some cases, an entire overnight rest. Afterward, the dry, crumbling paste is gently brushed or carefully washed away, revealing the design that had been concealed beneath it all along.

The skin beneath has now turned a genuinely rich reddish-brown color! This temporary stain will never remain on the skin indefinitely, since the pigment colors only the very outermost layer of skin cells before being shed away naturally over time.

People especially cherish using henna during joyful celebrations such as weddings and family gatherings, where the intricate designs frequently carry symbolic meanings of happiness or blessing, and many families also apply henna during the holiday of Eid.

After roughly one to three weeks, the henna pattern gradually and steadily fades away as old skin cells naturally wear off and are replaced by newer ones, and the skin eventually returns to its ordinary color once again, ready and waiting to be decorated anew for whatever celebration comes along next.

versions.title: Henna: An Enduring Art
versions.text:
Anyone who looks closely and carefully at the intricate red-brown patterns on a hand or foot can readily appreciate why henna remains among the most enduring and genuinely widespread forms of temporary body art practiced throughout much of the world, a venerable tradition originating from a flowering plant, Lawsonia inermis, that flourishes abundantly in warm climates across Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

To produce the dye, growers meticulously harvest the leaves of the henna plant and allow them to dry thoroughly and completely under the intense sun. Once fully dried, the leaves are then carefully ground into a fine, green powder containing a natural reddish-brown pigment called lawsone, which is responsible for the plant's distinctive staining properties and has been genuinely prized for countless centuries.

That pigment-rich powder is subsequently combined with ordinary water, and frequently a small amount of fresh lemon juice or strong tea, to produce a smooth, remarkably thick paste. This paste typically appears dark green or deep brown while still wet, long before it eventually and completely dries upon the skin's surface.

A genuinely skilled henna artisan carefully applies the paste onto a person's skin, meticulously piping it through a small cone or plastic bottle to render remarkably intricate, highly detailed patterns across the hands, feet, and sometimes even the forearms of the person being decorated. Producing these elaborate patterns can require a truly considerable investment of time and patience.

The paste must remain undisturbed on the skin sufficiently long to dry completely and properly set, a process that usually requires several hours or, in some cases, an entire overnight rest. Afterward, the dry, crumbling paste is gently brushed off or carefully washed away, revealing the design that had been concealed beneath it the entire time.

The skin beneath has now fully turned a genuinely rich reddish-brown color! This temporary stain will never remain on the skin indefinitely, since the pigment colors only the very outermost layer of skin cells before being shed away naturally over time.

People especially cherish using henna during joyful celebrations such as weddings and large family gatherings, where the intricate designs frequently carry symbolic meanings of happiness or blessing, and many families also apply henna during the holiday of Eid.

After roughly one to three weeks, the henna pattern gradually and steadily fades away as old skin cells naturally wear off and are continuously replaced by newer ones, and the skin eventually returns to its ordinary color once again, ready and patiently waiting to be beautifully decorated anew for whatever joyous celebration comes along next.

representing or standing for a deeper meaning

The pigment reacts almost instantly with ordinary water and completely dissolves away within seconds
